cues.text: Two Crowns
Born Raymund Kolbe in 1894 in Zduńska Wola, in Russian-controlled Poland, the future saint reported a vision at around age ten.
The Virgin Mary appeared to him, offering a choice between two crowns—one white, signifying purity, and the other red, signifying martyrdom.
Asked which he would accept, the boy said he chose both.
A Media Apostle of Mary
Entering the Conventual Franciscans as a teenager and taking the name Maximilian, Kolbe earned doctorates in philosophy and theology in Rome before returning to Poland.
There, he founded the Militia of the Immaculata , a movement promoting evangelization through consecration to Mary.
Remarkably for a friar of his era, he harnessed modern mass media — printing presses, radio, and eventually plans for aviation and film — to spread it.
The City of the Immaculata
In 1927, Kolbe founded Niepokalanów ('City of the Immaculata') near Warsaw, a vast Franciscan publishing center.
Within a dozen years, it grew from eighteen friars to over 650 members, producing a widely circulated magazine.
By the outbreak of war, it was one of the largest religious publishing operations in the world.
He also spent six years establishing a similar mission and publishing center in Nagasaki, Japan.
Sheltering the Persecuted
When Nazi Germany invaded Poland in 1939, Kolbe refused to sign documents claiming German ancestry that would have granted him privileged status under occupation.
Instead, he turned Niepokalanów into a refuge, sheltering as many as 3,000 displaced people, roughly half of them Jewish.
He provided food, clothing, and even facilities for Jewish religious observance under the friars' protection.
Arrest and Auschwitz
Kolbe was arrested by the Gestapo in February 1941 after continuing to publish material the Nazi authorities regarded as subversive, and was transported to Auschwitz in May of that year.
When three prisoners disappeared from his barracks that July, camp authorities selected ten men at random to be starved to death as reprisal and deterrence.
One selected man, Franciszek Gajowniczek, cried out in anguish over the wife and children he would leave behind.
Kolbe stepped forward and volunteered to take his place.
Legacy
Kolbe survived nearly two weeks in the starvation bunker, reportedly leading the other condemned men in prayer, before being killed by lethal injection on August 14, 1941 — the eve of the Assumption.
Canonized in 1982 by Pope John Paul II , who described him as 'the patron of our difficult century,' Kolbe is honored as a martyr of charity.
Franciszek Gajowniczek, the man whose life he saved, survived the war and was present at his canonization decades later.
